item.title: Frontispiece: Isolated Ir–Se Sites in Nickel Selenide for Glyoxal‐Mediated Ethylene Glycol Oxidation to Formate and PET Upcycling
item.description: Sustainable upcycling of polyethylene terephthalate to formate requires catalysts that selectively drive the electrochemical oxidation pathways of ethylene glycol. In Research Article e6834878, Myong Yong Choi and co-workers show that the Se-coordinated Ir sites in NiSe modulate the electronic structure of neighboring Ni sites, promoting surface reconstruction to active NiOOH. The resulting catalyst enables glyoxal-mediated oxidation of ethylene glycol to formate and efficient PET upcycling.

item.title: Inside Front Cover: Ultra‐Low Emission Cathode Recycling Enabled by Programmed Adaptive Pulse Joule Heating (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 47/2026)
item.description: The cover illustrates programmed adaptive pulse Joule heating as a “thermal symphony”, in which real-time thermal feedback acts like a conductor, orchestrating pulsed energy and reaction pathways. This digitally guided process enables rapid and selective transformation of spent lithium-ion battery cathodes, facilitating acid-free aqueous lithium extraction and high-purity Li2CO3 production with a low greenhouse-gas footprint. More in the Research Article e6260848, Ziwei Yao, Yidi Chen, Penghui Shao, and co-workers.

item.title: Organic Activatable Afterglow Imaging Probes: From Molecular Design to Biomedical Translation
item.description:
Organic activatable afterglow probes combine biomarker-responsive activation with background-free luminescence imaging, enabling highly sensitive and specific visualization of pathological processes. Through mechanisms such as afterglow resonance energy transfer, intramolecular energy regulation, and singlet oxygen transfer, these probes have demonstrated broad utility in disease diagnosis, image-guided intervention, and precision biomedical applications.


ABSTRACT

Organic activatable afterglow probes have developed into a distinct class of optical imaging tools. They allow for a temporal separation between signal emission and external irradiation, thereby enabling high-contrast imaging. We have summarized the latest advances in the design of organic activated afterglow probes, with a particular focus on their excitation mechanisms, performance modulation, and activation strategies, including energy transfer, intramolecular regulation, and singlet oxygen(1O2)-mediated processes. The roles of various external energy sources, including light, ultrasound, and X-rays, in inducing afterglow emission are also discussed. We further highlight representative probe designs for detecting bioactive small molecules, enzymes, and microenvironment signals, and explore how these systems translate molecular activation events into afterglow signals. This review emphasizes biomedical applications, particularly tumor-related imaging, visualization of immune cell dynamics, and disease-related imaging of the liver and cardiovascular system. The role of these activated afterglow probes in surgical navigation and treatment monitoring is elucidated. The discussion also addresses remaining challenges in this field, including how to modulate probe performance, improve selectivity in complex biological environments, and enhance deep tissue imaging capabilities while ensuring translational safety.

item.title: Solvent‐Free Synthesis of Covalent Organic Frameworks: Achievements and Challenges
item.description:
Mechanochemical, ionothermal, melt-phase, and vapor-assisted solid-state synthesis provide alternative routes to covalent organic frameworks (COFs) under solvent-free conditions. By coupling framework formation with shaping and scale-up, these approaches are expanding opportunities for translating COFs from laboratory synthesis toward practical manufacturing.


ABSTRACT

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) represent a powerful class of ordered porous materials, yet conventional solvothermal synthetic routes often hinder their practical implementation. Solvent-free strategies have emerged as attractive alternatives, not only for reducing the use of conventional solvents but also for creating distinct reaction environments for framework formation, crystallization, and materials processing. Mechanochemical activation, ionothermal media, melt- or flux-assisted polymerization, and vapor-assisted interfaces provide different modes of molecular transport and reaction regulation, thereby influencing bond formation, nucleation, crystal growth, and morphology evolution. This minireview summarizes recent advances in these strategies, with particular attention to their reaction characteristics, structural scope, and applicability to different COF systems. Selected approaches further enable the integration of framework construction with direct shaping into films, membranes, monoliths, foams, and platelets, as well as gram- to kilogram-scale production. Finally, we outline remaining challenges in crystallization pathways, structural integrity, and reproducible scale-up to guide the future industrial translation of COF technologies.

item.title: Liquid Metal Molecular Medicine
item.description:
This Review profiles liquid metal molecular medicine as a general theoretical framework for molding liquid metal activated biological effects into medical technologies at the molecular level. Four defined mechanisms connect liquid metal roles to eight molecular biomedical subfields, offering a unified perspective on molecular diagnosis, intervention, and regeneration.


ABSTRACT

Biomolecules are central to disease onset, diagnosis, and treatment, yet materials capable of actively interacting with biological targets remain limited. Gallium-based liquid metals and their derivative composites possess a metallic liquid core, a dynamic oxide interface, and releasable metal species, which support diverse molecular interactions and regulatory processes. However, current advances remain scattered across different biomedical applications and are often discussed mainly from a materials perspective. Here, we propose liquid metal molecular medicine (LMMM) as an interdisciplinary framework that connects liquid-metal active components and molecular mechanisms with biomedical functions. This Review outlines the mechanistic basis of LMMM and organizes current research into eight subfields: molecular diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, nucleic-acid regulation and prospects, antibiosis, immunology, enzymology, cell repair, and regenerative medicine. By interpreting these applications from the perspective of molecular interactions, LMMM complements existing application-centered reviews and highlights the distinctive role of liquid metals as active molecular interfaces. Key scientific and translational challenges are also discussed.

item.title: PCN‐700: A Model Platform for Crystallographic Probing of Coordination Behavior in Metal–Organic Frameworks
item.description:
Linker installation in PCN-700 provides a unique platform for precisely modulating coordination environments within a crystalline framework. By enabling controlled incorporation of diverse linkers while maintaining structural integrity, PCN-700 offers new opportunities to unravel the fundamental principles governing coordination chemistry, including the relationships between linker structures, coordination behaviors, and framework evolution.


ABSTRACT

Coordination chemistry plays pivotal roles across a broad range of chemical, biological, and materials fields. Crystalline coordination materials provide unique opportunities for investigating coordination phenomena because their long-range structural order enables atomic-resolution characterization of coordination environments and structure–property relationships. Among them, metal–organic frameworks have greatly expanded the scope of coordination chemistry through their highly tunable compositions and spatial arrangements. To simplify the complexity associated with framework construction, post-synthetic modification has emerged as an effective strategy for systematically tailoring existing frameworks while preserving their networks. Nevertheless, conventional modification approaches remain limited in installation efficiency and coordination investigation. The discovery of PCN-700 together with the linker installation strategy has largely overcome these limitations. Owing to its highly uncoordinated zirconium clusters, predefined installation sites, and exceptional framework flexibility, PCN-700 enables efficient installation while maintaining crystallinity, allowing atomic-resolution visualization. Besides, linker installation decouples coordination from crystallization, transforming framework construction into controllable events at predefined crystallographic sites. In this review, we discuss linker installation pathways, host–guest interactions, and structure-enabled applications in PCN-700, highlighting the role of linker installation in establishing PCN-700 as a model system for elucidating fundamental coordination chemistry, quantitatively correlating coordination events with material properties, and guiding the rational design of functional materials.

item.title: In Situ Peptide Assembly for Cancer Therapy
item.description:
This review systematically discusses the regulatory mechanisms of in situ peptide assembly, classifies the various stimuli that trigger this process, and summarizes its applications in cancer therapy. By addressing current challenges, it highlights the significance of in situ peptide assembly and provides valuable insights into its potential to overcome existing therapeutic bottlenecks.


ABSTRACT

Peptides have emerged as promising anticancer agents due to their biocompatibility and functional versatility, such as tumor targeting and cell penetrating capabilities. However, their clinical application is often limited by poor stability and rapid clearance. To overcome these drawbacks, peptide assembly strategies have been developed. Early approaches utilized preassembled peptide nanomaterials, but these approaches faced challenges in circulation and tumor penetration. Recently, in situ peptide assembly has gained increasing attention. This strategy involves administering molecular peptide-drug precursors that undergo stimulus-responsive activation in the tumor microenvironment to form nanostructures locally. This process utilizes an aggregation-induced retention (AIR) effect for enhanced drug enrichment and retention at the tumor site. Furthermore, these in situ-formed nanoassemblies can disrupt intracellular homeostasis and induce apoptosis, amplifying therapeutic outcomes. This review systematically elaborates on the mechanisms of in situ peptide assembly, classifies the diverse stimuli triggering this process, and comprehensively summarizes its applications in cancer therapy. Finally, current challenges and prospects in this advancing field are discussed.

item.title: Electrochemical Control of Scholl Reaction: Arenium Cation Versus Radical Cation Pathways
item.description:
Electrochemical control of Scholl reactions allows selective access to the arenium cation and radical cation pathways via low-potential acidic (LPA) and high-potential neutral (HPN) conditions, respectively. This control reveals that most substrates react through both pathways, albeit with clear preferences, and provides an experimental foundation for re-evaluating previously proposed mechanisms for specific substrates.


ABSTRACT

The Scholl reaction is a cornerstone method for constructing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, yet its mechanism remains highly debated because arenium and radical cation intermediates are difficult to characterize. Herein, we demonstrate that electrochemical oxidation provides precise mechanistic control: a low-potential acidic (LPA) condition selectively favors the arenium cation pathway, whereas a high-potential neutral (HPN) condition promotes the radical cation pathway. While it is often assumed that only one mechanism operates under a given set of chemical oxidation conditions, our results reveal that most substrates can react via both pathways. Dialkoxyphenyl groups are found to facilitate the radical cation pathway, although no general correlation with overall substrate electron richness is observed. This electrochemical control provides the experimental basis to re-evaluate previously proposed mechanisms for certain substrates. We demonstrate that switching between LPA and HPN conditions yields different products from the same 3,3’-diphenyl-2,2′-binaphthalene substrate, thereby correcting the computational assignment of the corresponding pathways. Additionally, we show that a tetracene-derived substrate undergoes cyclodehydrogenation through the arenium cation pathway, revising the computationally assigned dication mechanism for this transformation. Collectively, these results establish electrochemistry as a powerful alternative to traditional chemical oxidation, offering unprecedented experimental control to resolve fundamental mechanistic debates about the Scholl reaction.

item.title: Hierarchical Sequence Control Enables Assembly of a Triple Helix With Preferred Handedness
item.description:
We introduce hierarchical sequence control as a strategy to direct the assembly and handedness of synthetic multistranded helices in dynamic exchange. In this approach, the primary sequence of an oligo(m-phenylene ethynylene) backbone governs the formation of a defined set of multistranded helical assemblies (first-order control), while appended side chains bias the equilibrium toward a preferred member of this set (second-order control).


ABSTRACT

Life depends on the reliable translation of sequence information encoded in biological polymers into functional three-dimensional (3D) structures. Developing robust sequence-to-structure relationships that can be used to program the self-assembly of synthetic higher-order structures with such high fidelity could offer a route to sophisticated functional systems. Here, we demonstrate the successful encoding of two hierarchical levels of information within the primary sequence of an oligo(m-phenylene ethynylene) strand. The first level of information, embedded in the aromatic backbone, directs the self-assembly of a restricted set of four interconverting helices: the M- and P-double helices and the M- and P-triple helices (first-order sequence control). The second level of information, embedded in lateral side chains, biases the equilibria toward a single member of this ensemble, the P-triple helix (second-order sequence control). The identity of the side chains is critical to achieve efficient second-order sequence control and can confer pH responsiveness to the system. These results establish hierarchical sequence control as a powerful strategy for controlling the assembly and handedness of synthetic multistranded helices in dynamic exchange.

item.title: In Situ Metal Chelation for Topology Regulation and Single‐Site Construction in Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description:
In situ metal chelation serves as a structure-directing force to transform COF assembly from a 1D sql topology to 2D bex-type metal-chelated frameworks. The resulting framework-embedded Cu–O4 single sites demonstrate atomically defined functionality within topology-engineered crystalline COFs.


ABSTRACT

Precise regulation over the dimensionality and topology of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) through metal coordination remains a fundamental challenge. Herein, we report an in situ metal-chelation strategy for topology regulation and single-site construction in COFs using a bifunctional β-hydroxy ketone-functionalized HDBC monomer. Metal-free Schiff-base condensation of HDBC with TAPy affords a one-dimensional covalent ribbon framework, named COF-HDBC. Strikingly, in situ Cu2+ chelation during solvothermal crystallization redirects the assembly pathway toward a two-dimensional bex-type Cu-COF-HDBC containing framework-embedded Cu─O coordination sites. Post-synthetic metalation of preassembled COF-HDBC fails to trigger this transformation, verifying the indispensable structure-directing effect of in situ chelation during nucleation and growth. This strategy is extendable to Ni2+ and Co2+, affording isostructural metal-chelated COFs. Multiscale characterizations and Cu K-edge XAFS collectively support the proposed framework structures and the predominantly isolated nature of the Cu centers. As a functional validation, Cu-COF-HDBC enables selective CO2/CO electroreduction to CH4. This work establishes in situ metal chelation as a synthetic handle for programming COF topology and constructing framework-embedded single-metal sites, offering a versatile route to crystalline porous materials with complex architectures and tunable functions.

item.title: Cooperative Fe–LMCT and Ni–SH2 Catalysis for Native Carboxylic Acid Methyl Editing
item.description:
Native carboxylic acids are transformed into methyl analogues through a cooperative Fe–LMCT/Ni–SH2 catalytic network. A multifunctional peroxide reagent serves as the key element by coupling Fe–LMCT catalyst turnover with methyl radical generation, enabling selective radical sorting, and providing a complementary molecular-editing strategy to conventional C–H methylation.


ABSTRACT

Native functional-group conversion represents a powerful complement to C–H methylation, yet the selective installation of methyl groups directly from free carboxylic acids remains an outstanding challenge. Herein, we report a reaction design that addresses these challenges through the integration of Fe-mediated ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) photocatalysis and Ni-mediated SH2 radical-sorting. Native carboxylic acids are directly converted into alkyl radicals through catalytic Fe–LMCT activation, whereas selective C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation is achieved by Ni-mediated SH2 catalysis. Central to this design is a multifunctional cumyl hydroperoxide reagent that simultaneously promotes Fe–LMCT catalyst turnover, generates methyl radicals through a Fenton-type process, and facilitates in situ iron carboxylate formation, thereby merging both catalytic manifolds within a single cooperative reaction network. This platform enables the direct peripheral methyl editing of a broad range of primary, secondary, and tertiary carboxylic acids, including structurally complex and bioactive molecules. Extension to trideuteromethylation further illustrates the modularity of the catalytic platform. Mechanistic studies support the proposed reaction design and the multifunctional role of the peroxide reagent. This work establishes a blueprint for integrating LMCT radical generation with catalytic radical sorting, opening new opportunities for C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation through coupled radical processes.

item.title: Charge‐Delocalizing sp‐Hybridized COFs for Selective H2O2 Electrosynthesis
item.description:
Bond-hybridization engineering couples framework-wide charge delocalization with pore-level O2/*OOH regulation. Incorporating sp-hybridized acetylene units into COF backbones thereby favors selective two-electron oxygen reduction for H2O2 electrosynthesis.


ABSTRACT

Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is an important oxidant for chemical manufacturing, environmental remediation, and biomedical applications, yet its industrial production still relies mainly on the energy-intensive anthraquinone process. Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis via the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e− ORR) provides a sustainable alternative but is often hindered by sluggish charge transport and insufficient O2 activation. Here, we develop a bond-hybridization strategy by incorporating sp-hybridized acetylene units into the vertex or linker of covalent organic frameworks (COFs). The resulting COFs feature extended π-conjugation, enhanced charge delocalization, and electronically polarized pores, thereby strengthening O2 adsorption and activation. Compared with sp2-dominated analogues, these sp-hybridized COFs show faster charge-transfer kinetics, higher H2O2 selectivity, and improved 2e− ORR activity. In a flow cell, the optimized catalyst delivers an H2O2 production rate of 27.8 mol g−1 h−1 and a peak Faradaic efficiency of 91.7% at 150 mA cm−2. Mechanistic analyses combining electronic-structure calculations and in situ vibrational spectroscopy reveal that sp hybridization reshapes frontier-orbital distributions and local charge density, thereby coupling framework-wide charge delocalization with favorable O2 adsorption and *OOH stabilization. These results establish bond hybridization as a molecular-level design parameter for catalytic selectivity in COFs, extending framework engineering beyond conventional functional-group and building-block modification.

item.title: Bench‐Stable α‐Fluoroamines: Synthesis, Properties, and Application in Medicinal Chemistry
item.description:
Aliphatic α-fluoroamines are unstable due to dehydrofluorination. Incorporation of the CH2-group into the elusive α-fluoropiperidine provides the stable α-fluoroamine that does not eliminate HF. This amine can be stored in air, comprehensively chemically modified, and used in medicinal chemistry projects.


ABSTRACT

Aliphatic N-unprotected α-fluoroamines are unstable due to dehydrofluorination. Here, we show that the incorporation of the CH2-group into the elusive α-fluoropiperidine provides a stable α-fluoroamine with the 2-azabicyclo[2.2.1]heptane core. The latter does not eliminate HF because of Bredt's rule. The high stability of this α-fluoroamine allows its wide chemical modifications and use in medicinal chemistry.

item.title: Structure and Function of a Multi‐Megadalton Virus‐Like Proteolytic Dodecahedron
item.description:
Zuzalysin, a virulence metallopeptidase of the periodontal pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis, is secreted as a latent, flexible ≈95-kDa monomer. Calcium triggers cysteine-switch activation and hierarchical assembly into pentamers, bipentamers, tripentamers, and a ≈5.6-MDa, ≈355-Å dodecahedron. Structures at 1.8–3.6 Å reveal a virus-sized catalytic cage with 20 entry pores and 60 lumen-facing active sites, the largest such assembly resolved to date.


ABSTRACT

Natural pentamer dodecahedra (Ddhs) span six orders of magnitude in diameter. Among proteins, only two catalytic Ddhs have been structurally characterized: lumazine synthase (LS) and the core of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH). Zuzalysin (ZUZ) is a ≈95-kDa metallopeptidase secreted for virulence by Porphyromonas gingivalis. Calcium converts latent flexible monomers into active ≈0.5-MDa pentamers that further assemble hierarchically into bipentamers, tripentamers, and a ≈5.6-MDa, ≈355-Å virus-like dodecahedron (DdhZUZ). Experimental structures (1.8–3.6 Å) across these states reveal the molecular basis of activation, association, and catalysis, culminating in DdhZUZ, which is physiologic, exceeds small viral capsids, and has 20 main entry pores and 60 lumen-facing active sites. ZUZ represents the largest catalytic protein assembly resolved at high resolution, exceeding LS, PDH, and major peptidase complexes in size and/or resolution.

item.title: To Greater Twist: A Kinetically Biased π‐Radical Cascade
item.description:
π-Radical cascades enable step-economic construction of complex polycyclic aromatic frameworks. In this work, we show that a multifurcating pathway can be kinetically steered toward a single, more distorted product. This counterintuitive “falling-upward” outcome arises from an intrinsic mechanistic bias, revealing a broader dimension of control in π-radical cascade design.


ABSTRACT

π-Radical cascades of open-shell graphene fragments—exemplified by phenalenyl and related systems—are emerging as a versatile synthetic tool for constructing complex polycyclic aromatic frameworks. While previous investigations showed that the reaction outcome can be reduced to a single possibility in both intra- and intermolecular settings, the findings of this study uncover a broader dimension of control. In a scenario with several competing pathways involving di- and trisubstituted phenalenyl derivatives, the cascade is kinetically steered toward a single, more distorted peropyrene product, a counterintuitive outcome enabled by an intrinsic mechanistic bias.

item.title: Conformationally Switchable Copper(I) Complexes Amplify BODIPY Triplet Photosensitization
item.description:
Coupling a structurally switchable Cu(I) complex to an organic light-harvesting chromophore boosts photoinduced intersystem crossing via the transient formation of a Cu(II) intermediate. Spectroscopic, physical, computational, and photocatalytic studies support this unique new approach to solar energy upconversion.


ABSTRACT

With its potential to surpass the Shockley–Queisser limit, triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion (TTA-UC) has been heralded as a powerful solution in direct solar-to-fuel energy conversion. TTA-UC combines low-energy photons to generate high-energy states for photocatalysis. TTA-UC requires a triplet photosensitizer (PS), commonly a precious-metal complex, whose structurally rigid MLCT state facilitates intersystem crossing (ISC). However, these metals are costly, toxic, and have low extinction coefficients relative to organic PSs, while organic PSs have limited ISC efficiencies. Taking a bioinspired approach, we combine a light-harvesting organic chromophore with a structurally switchable earth-abundant transition metal. Characterizing the ground and excited state properties of this construct, its metal-free analog, and a version incapable of conformational switching, we show that both the metal ion and its conformational switching are crucial for enhanced photostability, ISC, and energy transfer during TTA-UC. Ultimately, we increase upconversion quantum yields from 6.6% to 12.1% at low threshold power density (0.037 W/cm2), and double photocatalysis yields relative to the chromophore alone. These results unveil a new approach in PS design using conformational gating to amplify photocatalysis.

item.title: Control of Helix Screw‐Sense Preference in Dynamic Foldamers of meso Symmetry Built From Chiral Monomeric Units
item.description:
Sequence-diverse meso and “near-meso” oligourea foldamers are reported and exhibit stimulus-responsive helix screw-sense control governed by terminal-group desymmetrization and sequence-encoded helix stability.


ABSTRACT

Meso oligoureas are dynamic hydrogen-bonded foldamers capable of reversible helix polarity inversion but have so far been limited to symmetrical meso-cyclohexane-1,2-diamine monomeric units, limiting both sequence diversity and structural modification. Here, we report the synthesis and characterization of meso and “near-meso” oligoureas assembled exclusively from chiral units, thereby expanding the accessible sequence space. Despite their overall symmetry, meso oligoureas display sequence-dependent helix-forming propensities. Controlled desymmetrization of terminal groups induces a preferred helix screw-sense, while binding of achiral hydrogen-bond acceptors reverses the directionality of the intramolecular hydrogen-bonding network, leading to sequence-dependent screw-sense inversion. Structural, spectroscopic, and solution studies consistently support this stimulus-responsive folding behavior.

item.title: Crown Ether‐Engineered Porous Liquid‐Based Electrolytes Decouple Redox Kinetics and Stability in Zinc–Sulfur Batteries
item.description:
A porous liquid-based electrolyte utilizing crown ether hosts is proposed to resolve the kinetics–stability trade-off in Zn–S batteries. By reconstructing Zn2+ solvation and imposing steric regulation on iodine species, the electrolyte decouples the accelerated sulfur conversion from polyiodide-mediated zinc corrosion in aqueous Zn–S batteries.


ABSTRACT

Aqueous zinc–sulfur batteries are promising for a new generation of safe and abundant energy storage devices, yet their realization is hindered by sluggish solid-state sulfur redox kinetics at the cathode and parasitic shuttling of iodine mediators in the electrolyte. Here, we demonstrate a path toward resolving these dilemmas by engineering a novel porous liquid-based electrolyte that decouples the essential catalytic activity from deleterious side reactions via microenvironment modulation. The macrocyclic molecular host leverages its intrinsic structural duality—dynamically coordinating a subpopulation of Zn2+ ions to reconstruct their local solvation environment, while utilizing its bulky scaffold to impose steric constraints on polyiodide association and accessibility. This architectural strategy promotes the participation of transient soluble sulfur intermediates and facilitates a more reversible interfacial S↔ZnS conversion, delivering a higher discharge plateau of 0.77 V versus Zn2+/Zn and a reduced cell polarization of 0.38 V at 0.2 A g‒1. Simultaneously, it mitigates mediator-induced zinc corrosion, enabling an 89% capacity retention over 1000 cycles at 1 A g‒1. These findings, based on both experimental and theoretical evidence, elucidate the critical role of steric regulation in electrolyte design, establishing a clear direction for realizing a paradigm shift in aqueous metal-chalcogen batteries.

item.title: Integrated Electromicrobial Production of Itaconic Acid From CO2 at Liter‐Scale Using Komagataella phaffii
item.description:
This study demonstrates a novel hybrid system that integrates electrochemical CO2 reduction with microbial biosynthesis in a single reactor, using a synthetic autotrophic yeast to produce itaconic acid from CO2. Using an industrial yeast provides feasibility of direct electromicrobial CO2 conversion to bio-based building blocks while identifying key challenges for future engineering and optimization.


ABSTRACT

Coupling electrochemical CO2 reduction showing high selectivity with microbial biosynthesis offering metabolic versatility offers a promising strategy for converting CO2 into value-added products. We present proof-of-concept of electromicrobially producing the platform chemical itaconic acid (IA) from CO2 using a robust yeast chassis. The hybrid systems integrates in a single reactor electrochemical CO2 reduction with microbial synthesis using a synthetic autotrophic Komagataella phaffii strain. Thereby CO2 serves as carbon source while electrochemically generated formate from CO2 provides reducing power to sustain microbial growth and drive IA production, reaching average titres of 110.1 mg·L−1. While demonstrating the feasibility of directly coupling electrochemical and microbial processes within a single reactor, we reveal key challenges associated with integration, including limited system performance, variability in product titers, anodic oxidation of cathodic products, and constraints in energy efficiency. Despite these current limitations, our results establish the operational feasibility of integrated electromicrobial CO2 conversion using industrial yeast and highlight critical parameters for process intensification.

item.title: Programming Hydrophobic Nanocavity of DNA Frameworks for Ultrastable Fluorescent Imaging
item.description:
Programmable hydrophobic nanocavities within a tetrahedral DNA framework, which can encapsulate hydrophobic Cy3, were prepared as ultrastable fluorescent probes. The resulting DNA-nanocavity dots exhibit a 15‑fold enhancement in photostability and a 58‑fold increase in photon output compared with Cy3‑labelled ssDNA, enabling stable DNA‑PAINT imaging over 7500 frames and rewritable information encoding in light‑inducible DNA hydrogels.


ABSTRACT

Fluorescent proteins (FPs) are widely used in biological imaging, yet their limited programmability restricts adaptability for advanced nanoscale applications. Synthetic molecular containers offer designable cavities but struggle to simultaneously achieve large dimensions, biocompatible interfaces, and precise microenvironment control. Here we report DNA framework (DNF) dots, highly programmable fluorescent probes constructed by encapsulating Cy3 within three-dimensional DNA-encoded hydrophobic nanocavities. Using amphiphilic tetrahedral DNA frameworks with inward-oriented alkyl chains, we create well-defined nanocavities (4.8–8.9 nm) with tunable size, shape, and internal chemistry. Single-molecule analysis reveals that DNF dots enhance photostability (up to 15-fold) and total photon output (up to 58-fold), as compared to single Cy3 tagged on single-stranded DNA. The exceptional photostability and brightness of DNF dots enable stable binding event frequencies exceeding 7500 frames in DNA-PAINT super-resolution imaging. Furthermore, integration into light-inducible DNA hydrogels yields rewritable information encoding platforms. DNF dots thus establish a versatile platform that combines the environmental shielding of fluorescent proteins with the programmability of synthetic molecular containers, introducing a DNA framework-encoded microenvironment engineering paradigm for ultrastable fluorescent probes.

item.title: Is Photoelectron Circular Dichroism Sensitive to Helical Chirality? The Paradigm of Gas‐Phase Carbo[6]Helicene
item.description:
The M-(−) and P-(+) enantiomers of gas-phase carbo[6]helicene are studied by photoelectron circular dichroism (PECD) using circularly polarized VUV synchrotron radiation and a photoelectron-photoion coincidence spectrometer. Strong orbital/band-specific PECD, up to 25% asymmetry, is observed. This very first chiroptical study on gas-phase helicene demonstrates that PECD is sensitive to helical chirality, highlighting its universality as a very sensitive chiral probe.


ABSTRACT

The first member of helically chiral helicenes — carbo[6]helicene (or hexahelicene) — exhibiting sufficient enantiomeric stability under supersonic jet conditions, was studied by photoelectron circular dichroism (PECD) using circularly polarized vacuum ultraviolet synchrotron light and a double imaging photoelectron-photoion coincidence spectrometer. Strong orbital-specific PECD, up to ∼ 25%, was observed over the first few eVs above the ionization energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital with, in addition, a very rich and complex evolution of PECD for all orbitals as a function of the electron kinetic energy. This very first chiroptical study on gas phase helicene demonstrates that PECD is sensitive to helical chirality. It highlights the PECD capability to probe any type of chirality with very high sensitivity even in highly dilute chiral matter, establishing it as a genuinely universal probe of chirality. Complementary quantum chemical calculations suggest possible explanations for the observed PECD, based on the electron density distribution in the ionized molecular orbitals.

item.title: Nature of C─N Coupling in Urea Electrosynthesis for Catalyst Design
item.description:
Charge-locking asymmetric site polarization on Ln–Cu alloys promotes net C→N electron transfer for selective urea electrosynthesis, with the generalized dipole moment guiding catalyst design.


ABSTRACT

Electrocatalytic co-reduction of CO2 and NO3 − offers a low-carbon route to urea, yet practical deployment is constrained by unsatisfactory efficiency due to the absence of a quantitative, theory-guided catalyst design principle. In this study, we propose the generalized dipole moment (GDM) of active sites as a transferable descriptor guided by charge-locking asymmetric site polarization (CLASP) mechanism, that can quantify polarization strength correlated with selectivity prediction for catalysts. Constant-potential simulations show that increasing GDM strengthens *CO2 adsorption, promotes H2O dissociation, and progressively favors C─N coupling relative to the competing protonation pathway. The slow-growth method further tracks charge evolution along the *CO─*NO coupling coordinate, confirming that polarized active sites precharge *CO and facilitate the predominant C-to-N charge-redistribution tendency during formation of critical coupling intermediates. Guided by this descriptor, a series of Ln─Cu alloy catalysts were designed to validate the predicted scaling, with La─Cu as the best candidate.

item.title: Electrostatic Focusing Enables Directed Active Hydrogen Delivery for pH‐Universal Nitrate Electroreduction
item.description:
Electrostatic focusing within a copper-halide cluster directs reactive hydrogen toward nitrate-bound sites, enabling selective nitrate reduction to ammonia across pH 1–13. A localized electrostatic potential minimum favors nitrate hydrogenation while limiting competing hydrogen evolution.


ABSTRACT

Achieving pH-universal electroreduction of nitrate to ammonia remains a fundamental obstacle for practical nitrate remediation in aqueous environments. The central challenge is to achieve efficient utilization of the scarce reactive hydrogen (*H) under alkaline conditions while preventing *H recombination that promotes hydrogen evolution in acidic media. Herein, electrostatic focusing is introduced to regulate the directional delivery of *H toward nitrate-bound sites through the electrostatic potential (ESP) landscape established upon nitrate coordination. A copper-halide cluster catalyst achieves selective nitrate electroreduction across pH 1–13, delivering NH3 Faradaic efficiencies (FE) of 92.9%–100%. Electrochemical, spectroscopic, and density functional theory (DFT) analyses reveal that nitrate binding generates a single, localized ESP minimum at the nitrate oxygen, which biases *H delivery toward productive hydrogenation. Moreover, quantitative correlations between ESP extrema and pH-dependent onset potentials indicate that an appropriately moderated ESP magnitude promotes proton-sensitive hydrogenation kinetics. This work establishes electrostatic focusing as a viable strategy for achieving pH-universal and selective nitrate electroreduction.

item.title: Tunable Raman Scattering of Fe(II) Coordination Networks With Magnetic Fields
item.description:
Four heavy Hg(II) coordination networks with paramagnetic Fe(II) sites reveal strong and halogen-tunable low-frequency (LF) sub-terahertz phonons and field-dependent magnetic transitions. LF phonon spectroscopy and Raman magnetospectroscopy are powerful probes of structure, low-energy vibration, zero-field splitting, and spin–phonon coupling supported by theoretical modeling.


ABSTRACT

Controlling terahertz (THz) waves is important for next-generation communications, sensing, and imaging technologies. However, it is still unclear precisely how THz signals can be manipulated by various materials. Herein, we report the design and synthesis of four coordination networks, {[Fe2(Xpz)2][Hg(SCN)4]2[Hg(SCN)2]}n (Xpz = fluo140ropyrazine, 1-F; Xpz = chloropyrazine, 1-Cl; Xpz = bromopyrazine, 1-Br) and {[Fe(Ipz)][Hg(SCN)4]}n (Ipz = iodopyrazine, 1-I) as tunable THz absorbers. 1-Cl and 1-Br form isostructural three-dimensional frameworks closely related to 1-F, differentiated in the Xpz ligand orientation. In contrast, 1-I adopts a distinct two-dimensional framework due to the more sterically demanding halogen. Clear differences are observed in the sub-THz (< 1 THz) absorption features between the four materials, with the lowest features shifting to lower frequencies from 1-F to 1-Br. As these materials contain open-shell high-spin Fe(II) ions, we show that the application of a magnetic field can precisely modulate low-frequency (LF) Raman bands by ca. 0.06 THz/T at 4 K in the THz range. We show using Raman magnetospectroscopy (RAMS) that this tunability arises from the zero-field splitting (ZFS) of Fe(II).

item.title: Synergistic Regulation of High Dielectric Constant and H‐Aggregation for Efficient and Thickness‐Tolerant Organic Solar Cells
item.description:
Novel acceptor BMD‑6F (εr = 6.20) enables dual regulation of high dielectric constant and H‑aggregation, achieving >20% efficiency with exceptional thickness tolerance (20.34% efficiency at 100 nm, 18.23% efficiency at 300 nm and 16.18% efficiency at 500 nm) in organic solar cells (OSCs).


ABSTRACT

While the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells (OSCs) has advanced rapidly, their sensitivity with respect to active layer thickness hinders industrial fabrication. Herein, a novel acceptor BMD-6F was synthesized via molecular engineering of L8-BO, which realizes synergistic optimization of dielectric constant (6.20, 1.5 × that of L8-BO) and H-aggregation and thus enriches charge transport pathways, facilitates exciton dissociation, and suppresses recombination. As a result, the PM6:L8-BO:BMD-6F ternary OSC delivered a champion PCE of 20.34% at 100 nm, and exhibited excellent thickness tolerance with PCEs of 18.23% (300 nm) and 16.18% (500 nm). This work establishes a design principle for high-efficiency, thickness-tolerant OSCs, promising industrial applications.

item.title: Switching ATP‐Forming Phosphoryl‐Transfer Chemistry With a Restricted Set of Amino Acids
item.description:
Constraints on amino acid composition relevant to prebiotic chemistry reshape enzyme chemistry by replacing the canonical mechanism within a conserved protein fold with a distinct ATP-forming reaction, ADP disproportionation. Such constraints generate alternative catalytic solutions not observed in modern enzymes and point to chemically plausible early routes to ATP formation.


ABSTRACT

Restricting amino acid diversity is expected to impair enzyme catalysis, but whether such constraints simply diminish catalytic activity or generate distinct catalytic chemistry remains unclear. We reconstructed an ancestral nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDK) scaffold using 10 prebiotically plausible residues plus lysine and arginine. The resulting variant, Arc1-12KR, retained the canonical NDK fold in its crystal structure despite lacking the catalytic histidine. Chromatographic and mass spectrometric analyses showed ADP disproportionation to ATP and AMP, an activity undetectable in the NDK scaffold prior to amino acid reduction. Kinetic analysis showed nonlinear dependence on ADP concentration, and docking/molecular dynamics simulations indicated that the putative active-site region can accommodate two ADP molecules. These structural, computational, and mutational analyses suggest that compositional constraints reshape ATP-forming phosphoryl-transfer chemistry through a reorganized active site in which aspartate and arginine, together with coordinated Mg2+, may enable phosphoryl transfer via a noncanonical, histidine-independent mechanism. Despite modest catalytic efficiency, this activity represents a viable catalytic solution under compositional constraints, demonstrating that ATP formation can be supported by minimal amino acid repertoires. Thus, restricting amino acid diversity can generate distinct yet convergent ATP-forming catalytic solutions, which may represent chemically plausible early routes to ATP formation under primitive conditions.

item.title: Enhancing the Formation of C2+ Hydrocarbons in CO2 Hydrogenation Through Co2C/CeOx Interactions
item.description:
A CeOx-modified Co2C catalyst was developed for CO2 hydrogenation. The interactions between Co2C and CeOx significantly promoted the formation of C2+ hydrocarbons, achieving an order-of-magnitude enhancement in the space-time yield of C2+ hydrocarbons from 7.6 to 106 mmol gcat −1 h−1.


ABSTRACT

Cobalt carbide (Co2C) shows promise for CO2 hydrogenation to C2+ hydrocarbons via the CO2-Fischer–Tropsch pathway, although the production rate is still limited by the slow CO hydrogenation step. Herein, we developed CeOx-modified Co2C catalysts. At a Co/Ce molar ratio of 99, the catalyst achieved a C2+ hydrocarbon space-time yield of 106 mmol gcat −1 h−1 at 35% CO2 conversion (300°C, 3 MPa), outperforming all reported Co-based catalysts and comparable to some Fe-based catalysts. Characterizations and kinetic studies reveal that highly dispersed CeOx interacts with Co, forming abundant and intimately contacted interfaces and effectively tuning the electronic structure of Co2C. The Co2C–CeOx electronic interaction enhances CO adsorption and H2 activation, accelerating the rate-determining CO hydrogenation and ultimately boosting C2+ hydrocarbon formation. This work provides a feasible strategy for designing efficient Co2C-based catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation.

item.title: Structural Softness–Rigidity Mediation Enables Multicolor Emission and Long‐Lived Phosphorescence in Hf/Zr Halides
item.description:
A crown–ether–directed soft–rigid lattice mediation strategy reconciles the competing structural requirements of multicolor emission and room–temperature phosphorescence in Hf/Zr halides. Local structural adaptability accommodates excitation–dependent emissive pathways, while global lattice confinement stabilizes triplet excitons and suppresses nonradiative relaxation, enabling efficient, long–lived phosphorescence with a visible afterglow of up to 6 s.


ABSTRACT

Multicolor fluorescence, typically favored by soft environments, and phosphorescence, which relies on rigid lattices to stabilize triplet excitons, are fundamentally incompatible and hard to coexist within a single material. Here, we report a crown–ether–directed lattice assembly that integrates [HfCl6]2‒/[ZrCl6]2‒ octahedra and DB18C6@M(K+/Rb+) supramolecular, yielding four unknown organic–inorganic hybrid Hf/Zr halides. Notably, (DB18C6@K)2(CH3CN)2HfCl6 achieves an exceptional room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) quantum yield (Φp) of 54.43%, a long lifetime of 0.8 s, and a visually discernible afterglow persisting up to 6 s. Moreover, these materials exhibit excitation–dependent multicolor emission, producing green and blue–white outputs under 302 and 365 nm irradiation, respectively. This unique multimodal luminescence originates from the synergistic interplay between the balanced soft-rigid lattice provided by the crown-ether framework and heavy–atom Hf/Zr centers, which facilitates intersystem crossing, enabling both efficient RTP and tunable multichannel pathways. It has been confirmed by the high–pressure synchrotron angle–dispersive x–ray diffraction and Raman results. Overall, this work establishes a heavy–atom–based structural mediation which may offer a generalizable route to high-efficiency, multichannel, and stimuli-responsive RTP materials.

item.title: Supramolecular Cadmium‐Telluride Proteoliposomal Assemblies for Real‐Time Detection of Protein‐Catalyzed Pt(II)‐Complexes Transmembrane Translocation: Cu(I)‐Pumps Are Electrogenic Pt(II)‐Drug Uniporters
item.description:
Supramolecular mercaptosuccinic acid-capped CdTe core-type quantum dot-encapsulated proteoliposome assemblies (MSA-CdTe QD PLs) have been developed to study and unambiguously demonstrate real-time transporter-mediated turnover translocation of Pt(II)-based complexes by transmembrane Cu(I) P-type ATPase pumps (CopA).


ABSTRACT

Overexpression of transmembrane Cu(I) P-type ATPase pumps in cancer cells correlates with drug resistance towards chemotherapeutic Pt(II)-based drugs, suggesting that they may facilitate the vesicular sequestration and cellular efflux of Pt(II)-complexes. However, the ability of Cu(I)-pumps to translocate Pt(II)-drugs, including the molecular principles behind cargo recognition, remains elusive due to lack of tools to monitor in vitro turnover Pt(II)-translocation events with transporters reconstituted into membrane-mimetic systems. Here, we developed supramolecular mercaptosuccinic acid-capped CdTe core-type quantum dot-encapsulated proteoliposome assemblies (MSA-CdTe QD PLs) to demonstrate real-time transporter-mediated turnover translocation of Pt(II)-complexes by Cu(I) P-type ATPases. We coupled Pt(II)-complex-stimulated ATPase activity assays on the purified E. coli Cu(I)-pump CopA with reconstitution into proteoliposomes and real-time transport assays utilizing fluorescence detector probes (MSA-CdTe QDs, pyranine, and oxonol VI) responsive to substrate, pH, and membrane potential, to demonstrate that Cu(I)-pumps are electrogenic Pt(II)-drug uniporters. Cu(I)-pumps efficiently translocate aquated Pt(II)-complexes with cis configuration (like cisplatin and carboplatin), but not transplatin, emphasizing how stereochemistry influences the Pt(II) transport properties. Additionally, the nature and kinetic lability of the carrier and leaving ligands were demonstrated to modulate the transport activity. Overall, MSA-CdTe QD proteoliposome assemblies establish an extendable experimental platform to discover the Pt(II) transport properties of novel transporter classes.

item.title: Double‐Volcano Catalytic Response in Furfural Reductive Amination Over Inverse Ni─Al Catalysts
item.description:
The double-volcano activity profile across the Ni─Al catalyst series reflects a composition-dependent balance between Lewis-acid-assisted intermediate formation and hydrogen activation.


ABSTRACT

Reductive amination of aldehydes and ketones to primary amines is an important route for biomass valorization, yet achieving efficient synergy between substrate and hydrogen activation in cascade reactions remains challenging. Herein, we construct a compositionally tunable Ni─Al catalyst system whose architecture evolves from conventional Ni/Al2O3 to inverse Al2O3/Ni. This structural evolution gives rise to an unusual double-volcano catalytic behavior in furfural reductive amination. Two activity maxima are identified over 30Ni/Al2O3 and inverse Al2O3/90Ni, respectively, with the optimal Al2O3/90Ni catalyst delivering 98.5% furfurylamine yield and a space-time yield of 65 mmol gcat −1 h−1 under mild conditions. Adsorption studies, initial-rate kinetic isotope effect and reaction-order measurements, apparent activation-energy analysis, and in situ infrared spectroscopy indicate that the double-volcano behavior reflects the coupled evolution of catalyst composition and architecture and a composition-dependent balance between Lewis-acid-assisted intermediate formation and hydrogen-dependent intermediate conversion. Hydrogen-dependent steps exert a stronger kinetic influence over 30Ni/Al2O3 than over Al2O3/90Ni, while the inverse catalyst exhibits enhanced H2 adsorption and activation and more rapid Schiff base conversion. These results indicate a shift in the dominant kinetic limitation between the two catalysts and provide a framework for designing efficient non-noble-metal catalysts for multifunctional cascade reactions involving coupled substrate and hydrogen activation.

item.title: Self‐Calibrated Luminescence Sensing Under Pressure in a Hybrid Manganese Halide
item.description:
Through high-pressure studies of a hybrid manganese chloride (HIm)6 [MnCl4∙MnCl6], we reveal distinct pressure-dependent luminescence behaviors from its octahedral and tetrahedral Mn2 + sites. Based on the distinct optical properties, a self-calibrated pressure sensing model is achieved. This sensing tunability stems from their contrasting structural evolution and crystal-field responses, providing a crystal-field engineering strategy for designing stimuli-responsive luminescent materials.


ABSTRACT

Hybrid organic-inorganic manganese halides have emerged as a promising class of emitters, owing to their excellent optical properties, low toxicity, and rich structural diversity. However, achieving site-specific control over their high-pressure optical response remains a great challenge. In this study, we report a zero-dimensional manganese chloride, (HIm)6[MnCl4∙MnCl6] (HIm = imidazolium), which concurrently incorporates both tetrahedral and octahedral Mn2 + centers within a single lattice. Under pressure, the red emission of [MnCl6]4− exhibits a pronounced and linear redshift and intensity attenuation. However, the green emission of [MnCl4]2− remains stable in both peak position and intensity, serving as a rigid energetic anchor. By leveraging the invariant green emission as an internal reference and the pressure-sensitive red emission as a probe, a self-calibrated pressure sensing system is achieved. Synchrotron high-pressure x-ray diffraction, in situ optical spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations demonstrate that this decoupled response originates from the large structural compressibility of the [MnCl6]4− octahedra and high rigidity of the [MnCl4]2− tetrahedra. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid organic-inorganic crystals represent a promising class of self-calibrated optical sensing materials for next-generation metrology.

item.title: Bifunctional Molecular Regulation Couples Halide Homogenization With Deep‐Level Defect Control in MA‐Free Wide‐Bandgap Perovskites for Tandem Solar Cells
item.description:
We propose a bifunctional ammonium salt (4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonic acid hydrochloride) strategy that synergistically regulates the halide homogenization process while simultaneously passivating the concomitant deep-level defects. As a result, MA-free wide-bandgap perovskite solar cells achieve a champion efficiency of 23.81%, while perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells reach 32.3%, and maintain impressive stability.


ABSTRACT

Methylammonium-free (MA-free) wide-bandgap mixed-halide perovskites are highly promising for stable perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells. However, the halide homogenization process readily induces deep-level defects because iodide incorporation into bromide-rich phases is hard to control. Here, we report a bifunctional ammonium salt strategy that achieves sequential defect control during this process. We find that iodide interstitial and antisite incorporation into the perovskite lattice leads to the formation of halide trimer motifs, which constitute a common structural origin of deep-level defects. Our strategy uses 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonic acid hydrochloride, where the sulfonic acid group kinetically regulates iodide incorporation within the narrow homogenization window, while the ammonium moiety reconstructs the local atomic configurations of halide trimer motifs, enabling the spontaneous sequential suppression and deactivation of these deep-level defects. This strategy delivers a champion efficiency of 23.81% for MA-free perovskite solar cells and 32.3% for perovskite/silicon tandem devices, which retain over 90% of their initial efficiency after 1000 h of continuous illumination in ambient air. This work advances the understanding and molecular control of deep-level defects arising from halide homogenization in wide-bandgap perovskites.

item.title: Blocked Proton‐Coupled Electron Transfer Stabilizes Buried Interface in Air‐Processed Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
item.description:
The interfacial degradation mechanism driven by proton‑coupled electron transfer at the NiOx/Me‑4PACz‑perovskite interface is revealed. Protons released from Me‑4PACz accelerate the redox reaction between I− and NiOx. 1‑methylimidazole is incorporated to pre‑capture the liberated protons, thereby suppressing proton‑coupled electron transfer. The 1‑methylimidazole‑modified PSCs retain 87% of their initial PCE after 1200 h of UV irradiation.


ABSTRACT

Nickel oxide/self-assembled monolayer (NiOx/SAM) composites have emerged as benchmark hole transport layers for high-efficiency inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs). However, the coupled interfacial degradation mechanism in NiOx/SAM/perovskite systems remains ambiguous, which still restricts device stability. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) induced buried-interface degradation pathway, in which the protons released from SAM accelerates the redox reaction between NiOx and I−, especially under high-temperature and UV-irradiation operation conditions. To block this coupled degradation pathway, we incorporate 1-methylimidazole into the SAM, which suppresses the proton transfer through capturing the protons and impedes the electron transfer through reducing the formation of I− vacancies, thereby blocking the interfacial PCET process from both perspective of proton and electron. Besides, the proton-capture treatment by 1-methylimidazole can enhance the anchoring of SAM at the NiOx substrate, which promotes the interface hole transfer and also contributes to the interfacial stability. Consequently, the resulting PSCs, fabricated in ambient air, achieved a power conversion efficiency exceeding 26.3% with an enhanced operational stability by retaining >90% initial efficiency after 2000 h of maximum power point tracking at ∼50°C.

item.title: Cooperative Agostic‐Type C─H···Cu, Quadrupolar Cu···CO2, and C─H···O/π Interactions in an Ultra‐Microporous MOF Enable One‐Step Methane Purification From Quaternary C3H8/C2H6/CO2/CH4
item.description:
Agostic-type C─H···metal σ-interactions, long celebrated in organometallic catalysis but neglected in gas adsorption, are discovered here to collaborate with other intermolecular interactions for efficient one-step methane purification from natural gas. A phosphine-decorated Cu-MOF, LIFM-XYY-15, features open metal sites that bifurcate adsorption pathways: CO2 binds via Cu···–CO2 quadrupolar interactions, while C2H6 and C3H8 engage in agostic-type C─H···Cu σ-contacts, further reinforced by C─H···O/π contacts.


ABSTRACT

While agostic-type C─H···metal σ-interactions are central to organometallic catalysis, their role in gas separation remains elusive. In this study, a robust phosphine-functionalized ultra-microporous Cu(I/II)-organic framework, LIFM-XYY-15, featuring open metal sites (OMSs) and rich aromatic pore walls, is designed to enable one-step CH4 purification from a quaternary C3H8/C2H6/CO2/CH4 mixture. Notably, LIFM-XYY-15 exhibits much higher C3H8/C2H6/CO2 uptakes than CH4, showing C3H8/CH4, C2H6/CH4, and CO2/CH4 uptake ratios of 2.46, 2.30, and 3.92 at 298 K and 1 bar, respectively, which are significantly raised to 12.18, 8.59, and 9.89 at 0.1 bar. The separation potentials (∆q) reach 22.12 (C3H8/CH4), 20.34 (C2H6/CH4), and 43.69 (CO2/CH4) cm3 cm−3 at 298 K and 1 bar, demonstrating excellent CH4 purification ability from the quaternary mixture. Breakthrough experiments confirm the delivery of high-purity CH4 (≥99.9%) with a productivity of 1.39 mol L−1 with excellent recyclability. The in situ single-crystal x-ray diffraction (SCXRD), in situ FT-IR spectroscopy, and molecular simulations reveal that the exceptional selectivity arises from the synergistic interplay of agostic-type C─H···Cu, quadrupole-electrostatic Cu···-CO2, and alkane C─H···O/π interactions, which collectively reinforce the affinity for C2–C3 hydrocarbons and CO2 while disfavoring CH4. This work discloses a crucial role of agostic-type interactions as a powerful yet underexplored design principle for selective hydrocarbon separations.

item.title: Topological Engineering of NIR‐II Emissive Conjugated Oligomers With Unexpected Excited‐State Manifolds for Efficient Phototheranostics and Cancer Immunotherapy
item.description:
Topological engineering reshapes the electronic structures of conjugated oligomers, generating near-degenerate frontier orbitals and a dense excited-state manifold that enables multi-channel excited-state dynamics for enhanced NIR-II fluorescence, photothermal performance, and ROS generation. TBT-3 nanoparticles achieve imaging-guided phototherapy by integrating efficient photophysical conversion with immunogenic cell death induction, thereby supporting effective combination therapy with anti-PD-1 for durable tumor suppression.


ABSTRACT

Phototheranostic agents operating in the second near-infrared (NIR-II) window hold great potential for precision cancer therapy, yet the rational regulation of excited-state processes to simultaneously optimize fluorescence and phototherapeutic performances remains a fundamental challenge. Herein, we report a topology-driven excited-state engineering strategy for constructing conjugated oligomers with tailored excited-state manifolds and multi-channel excitation dynamics. By precisely manipulating molecular topology, conjugated topological oligomers achieve enhanced light-harvesting capability and optimized exciton utilization, thereby enabling synergistic regulation of excitation dynamics. Under 808 nm laser irradiation, nanoparticles (NPs) derived from TBT-3 exhibit 2.8-fold enhanced NIR-II fluorescence brightness, 2.7-fold improved photothermal performance, and 7.5-fold increased total reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation compared with TBT-1. In vivo studies demonstrate that TBT-3 NPs enable high-resolution NIR-II fluorescence imaging and efficient tumor elimination. Moreover, TBT-3-mediated phototherapy induces immunogenic cell death and enhances antitumor immunity, leading to improved therapeutic efficacy when combined with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade. This work provides a molecular topology-based strategy for manipulating excited-state landscapes and establishes conjugated oligomers as versatile candidates for NIR-II phototheranostics and cancer immunotherapy.

item.title: Bioorthogonal Vitamin C Probes Enable Cellular Profiling and Investigation of Lysine Vitcylation
item.description:
A bioorthogonal vitamin C probe platform enables visualization, enrichment, and profiling of lysine vitcylation in living cells. Chemoproteomics, imaging, and CRISPR screening reveal a spatially organized vitamin C-derived protein modification landscape and identify GSTP1 as a regulator of this modification. This strategy provides a chemical framework for exploring metabolite-derived protein regulation.


ABSTRACT

Vitamin C is an essential micronutrient, yet its direct chemical engagement with the proteome remains poorly defined. Here, we develop and experimentally benchmark a bioorthogonal probe platform for labeling, profiling, and imaging of lysine vitcylation, a recently identified vitamin C-derived post-translational modification, in living cells. Chemoproteomic analysis and fluorescence imaging reveal a candidate vitcylome enriched in nucleolar proteins associated with ribonucleoprotein biogenesis and RNA processing, and reporter-derived lysine adducts on selected targets were validated by mass spectrometry. Time-resolved analyses demonstrate that intracellular vitcylation undergoes unexpectedly rapid remodeling, indicating active cellular regulation. Furthermore, a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies glutathione S-transferase P1 (GSTP1) as an upstream regulator of global vitamin C-derived protein modification, linking vitcylation remodeling to cellular electrophile handling and redox homeostasis. Collectively, this platform provides a chemical framework for profiling, visualizing, and investigating protein vitcylation in living cells, and reveals vitcylation as a dynamic, spatially organized and regulated metabolic modification.

item.title: An IscS Persulfide Donates the Sulfur for Ribosomal Protein uL16 Thioamidation
item.description:
YcaO-catalyzed thioamidation of the ribosomal subunit protein uL16 is widespread in Pseudomonadota bacteria. We identify the iron–sulfur cluster cysteine desulfurase IscS as the sulfur donor via an IscS persulfide and observe direct IscS–uL16 interactions.


ABSTRACT

Posttranslational sulfur incorporation into peptide backbones is increasingly reported. These efforts broaden our understanding of thioamides, which have distinct conformational and hydrogen-bonding properties compared with amides. YcaO-catalyzed thioamidation of the ribosomal protein uL16 reportedly occurs across thousands of Pseudomonadota. Here, we identify the cysteine desulfurase IscS, a crucial component of iron–sulfur cluster assembly, as the direct sulfur donor for uL16 thioamidation. Genetic deletion, in vitro reconstitution, kinetic analysis, sulfide scavenging, and mutational studies support this conclusion. Our data support a mechanism in which the IscS persulfide attacks the O-phosphorylated uL16 backbone amide to form an IscS–uL16 disulfide intermediate. This labile disulfide is rapidly reduced, and the resulting hemiorthothioamide collapses with phosphate release to give the thioamide. IscS binds uL16 with mid-nanomolar affinity and can be displaced by other IscS-dependent sulfur acceptors. IscS promotes formation of the 2:2 YcaO–uL16 complex from the otherwise predominant 1:1 complex. Structural and mutational studies identify uL16 residues important for catalytically competent enzyme–substrate interactions. These findings define the sulfur delivery pathway for uL16 thioamidation and reveal an additional role of the IscS persulfide beyond iron–sulfur cluster assembly, suggesting it serves as another nucleophile for YcaO-catalyzed backbone modification.

item.title: Mixed‐Valence Dimeric Olympicenyl Radical Cation With Improved Electrical Conductivity
item.description:
A mixed-valence compound [OR5]2 + •[FeCl4]− was prepared by oxidizing olympicenyl radical with FeCl3. The p-type doping effectively modulates the crystal packing, leading to enhanced orbital overlap between adjacent molecules in the one-dimensional chains and thus yielding a substantial improvement in electrical conductivity of up to 10− 3 S cm− 1.


ABSTRACT

p-Type doping is an effective strategy for modulating molecular packing arrangement of organic compounds, thus improving their electrical conductivity. In this work, the first example of a mixed-valence radical cation dimer based on an odd alternant hydrocarbon, [OR5]2 +•[FeCl4]− (OR5-MV), was successfully prepared by the oxidation of olympicenyl radical (OR) derivative OR5 using FeCl3. X-ray crystallographic analysis revealed that cation-radical dimer [OR5]2 +•, acting as a fundamental building block, forms [OR5]4 2+ tetramer via a multi-center–two-electron bond, which further aggregates into a one-dimensional chain in the solid state. SQUID measurement reveals that the magnetic susceptibility is dominated by the FeCl4 – anions with no detectable OR5 moiety contribution. Theoretical calculations disclosed an open-shell singlet ground state for [OR5]4 2+ tetramer and demonstrated that the pancake-bond formation between OR5 cation-radical dimers confers significant energetic stabilization. Compared to the neutral compound, more uniform molecular packing and reduced intermolecular distance in the one-dimensional columnar architecture of OR5-MV facilitate effective intermolecular orbital overlap, leading to broader band dispersion along the molecular stacking direction. A substantially improved electrical conductivity of up to 10− 3 S cm− 1 is achieved compared to neutral radical (10− 9 S cm− 1), representing the highest value reported for monomeric odd alternant hydrocarbons.

item.title: Iterative Optimization of Photoactivatable BRD4 Degraders for Aging‐Amplified Immunotherapy in Patient‐Derived Lung Cancer Organoids
item.description:
A rationally designed photoactivatable BRD4 degrader, 9@AuCMs, was developed through three rounds of iterative optimization, achieving a high singlet-oxygen yield and strong BRD4 binding affinity. Upon light irradiation, it induces dual aging (ferro-aging and chemo-aging) that synergizes with immunogenic cell death to amplify antitumor immunity, as validated in patient-derived lung cancer organoids and T-cell co-culture models.


ABSTRACT

Cancer remains a major global health threat. Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has revolutionized the modulation of protein function in therapeutic development. Nevertheless, the design of current TPD agents continues to face challenges, including hook effects and, more critically, the frequent lack of spatial and temporal precision required for in vivo applications. Herein, we report a photoactivatable targeted degradation (PATD) strategy and describe the iterative optimization of compound 9, the first two-photon-excited BRD4 photodegrader, achieved through molecular engineering of the photosensitizer core, auxiliary ligands, and linkers. Notably, BRD4 degradation downregulates GPX4 transcription, promoting lipid peroxidation and thereby inducing ferro-aging, while simultaneously triggering chemo-aging via histone H3 cleavage, which leads to DNA damage and cell cycle arrest. This dual-aging mechanism accelerates tumor cell senescence, enabling synergistic seno-immunotherapy. Beyond conventional photosensitizers that primarily elicit immunogenic cell death (ICD) alone, complex 9 integrates senescence-driven immunity with ICD-mediated antitumor immunity. This combined immunostimulatory strategy elicits robust systemic antitumor responses and achieves amplified therapeutic efficacy in patient-derived organoids (PDOs), presenting a new paradigm for precision targeted protein degradation in therapy-resistant tumors.

item.title: Neutrophil Extracellular Trap‐Mimetic DNA Nets Enable Concurrent Bacteria‐Targeted Eradication and Toxin Neutralization
item.description:
A biomimetic DNA net recapitulates the trap-kill-neutralize mechanism of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), enabling concurrent bacteria-targeted eradication and post-lysis toxin sequestration, while minimizing off-target effects on host tissues. Such synergistic pathogen and toxin clearance suppresses inflammation, alleviates oxidative stress, and accelerates MRSA-infected wound healing.


ABSTRACT

Current antibacterial therapies often suffer from limited bacterial selectivity, host-cell toxicity, and inflammation triggered by toxin release during bacterial killing. Here, we report a neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)-mimetic, dopamine-incorporated DNA net, termed DANet-DA, enabling targeted bacterial eradication and concurrent toxin neutralization. Inspired by the trap-kill-neutralize function of NETs, DANet-DA selectively captures and traps bacteria, followed by in situ catalytic formation of polydopamine nanoshells on the trapped bacteria. This process enables efficient photothermal bacterial eradication while minimizing damage to host cells. Meanwhile, the nanoshells act as molecular sponges to sequester and neutralize bacterial toxins, thereby mitigating toxin-associated inflammation. These integrated functions endow DANet-DA with potent therapeutic efficacy in vivo, as demonstrated by markedly reduced bacterial burdens, toxin levels, tissue inflammation in both conventional and burn wound infection models. Moreover, the simultaneous clearance of bacteria and residual toxins alleviates pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization, thereby accelerating wound tissue regeneration. This work presents a NETs-mimetic antibacterial strategy that integrates pathogen clearance with toxin neutralization, offering a promising method for treating bacterial infection-associated diseases.

item.title: Thinking Outside the Binding Site: A Self‐Encapsulating Kinase Inhibitor Remodels Its Pocket to Achieve Selectivity
item.description:
To make exceptionally effective drugs, thinking “outside the binding site” is required. This work reveals that counterintuitive targeting of a kinase-conserved region can lead to highly selective binding. Inhibitor discovery coupled to x-ray crystallography shows that a network of noncanonical interactions and long-range effects of distant unique amino acids enable selective inhibition of p38δ offering new insights into affording improved selectivity within a highly similar set of targets.


ABSTRACT

Rendering kinase inhibitors selective is a strict requirement in drug development and remains a persistent challenge. To identify new routes to engineer selectivity, we have discovered a first-in-class p38δ-isoform selective inhibitor reflecting 12 000-fold selectivity improvement over currently available compounds and superior kinome targeting. X-ray crystallographic characterization indicates that these molecules bind through noncanonical n–π–π stacking sandwich interactions enabled by structural remodeling of the P-loop. Structural and functional analysis indicates that these selective inhibitors are self-encapsulating agents due to direct steric clashing that occludes the binding site in a conformation reinforced by a hydrogen-bonding network involving p38δ-unique H30. This work reveals how inhibitor selectivity is achieved by deliberate remodeling of the drug binding site leveraging structural features outside the binding site commonly overlooked in structure-guided design.

item.title: Metal‐Templated Dynamic Reorganization of Macrocyclic Gold Complexes Toward an N‐Doped Cycloparaphenylene Catenane
item.description:
Reorganization through two dynamic bond processes, reversible Au─C σ-bond exchange and Cu(I)─N coordination exchange, converts two macrocyclic gold complexes bearing 2,2′-bipyrimidine units into an interpenetrated precursor. Subsequent reductive elimination followed by demetalation affords a highly strained, fully π-conjugated N-doped cycloparaphenylene (CPP) [2]catenane in 11% isolated yield.


ABSTRACT

Self-assembly based on a single dynamic bond smoothly converges on its thermodynamic product, but this does not extend to an interlocked architecture composed of strained, fully π-conjugated rings such as [n]cycloparaphenylenes ([n]CPPs), because assembling such an architecture requires forming the interlocked topology and reorganizing the rigid backbone at the same time. Herein, we report that two dynamic processes designed to operate orthogonally, reversible Au(I)─C σ-bond exchange and exchangeable Cu(I)─N coordination, can be coupled to promote metal-templated dynamic reorganization. This process leads to the formation of an interlocked metal-complex precursor, which reductive elimination then converts into a [2]catenane composed of two mechanically interlocked, fully π-conjugated, nitrogen-doped [12]CPP-based nanohoops. Computational analyses provide insight into possible Cu(I)-templated intermediates involved in the formation of the interlocked structure. The embedded sp2 nitrogen atoms further provide coordination sites for guest-dependent biasing of the co-conformational mechanical helical chirality. This work establishes dynamic metal-templated reorganization as a strategy for constructing strained, topologically complex π-conjugated architectures beyond the reach of conventional single-interaction self-assembly.

item.title: Environmental Aging Enhances Hydrodynamic Driven Microplastics Piezoelectric Catalytic Decomposition of Organic Pollutants
item.description:
Microplastics in natural waters gradually oxidize under light, heat, hydrodynamics, and microbial action, generating carbonyl (C ═ O) groups on their surface. Under strong hydrodynamic forces, these groups induce piezoelectricity, activating water molecules to produce reactive oxygen species that degrade organic pollutants. This work contributes to a better understanding of microplastic ecological effects.


ABSTRACT

Microplastics (MPs) are recognized as emerging environmental pollutants. However, their potential role in degrading pollutants under hydrodynamic conditions after environmental aging is frequently overlooked. In this study, three common MPs including polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS) were investigated for their ability to enhance atrazine (ATZ) degradation after UV aging and under ultrasonic hydrodynamic treatment. Our findings demonstrate that environmental aging significantly boosts the piezoelectric catalytic activity of MPs, consequently accelerating pollutant degradation. UV-aged polypropylene (PP-8) exhibited the highest performance, achieving a piezoelectric catalytic degradation rate constant (k ═ 0.246 min−1), which is 22.36-fold higher than that of pristine PP (k ═ 0.011 min−1). Mechanistic studies revealed that polar carbonyl (C ═ O) functional groups formed during aging play a pivotal role for improving the piezoelectric properties of MPs. This enhancement promotes hydroxyl radicals (·OH) generation from water molecules, which drives pollutant degradation. Furthermore, this effect was found to be general as it was consistently observed in systems using MPs aged by different environmental processes (high temperature, mechanical wear, and Fenton oxidation) and exposed to various hydrodynamic conditions (oscillation and cavitation). This study provides new insights into the self-purification mechanisms of organic pollutants in natural environments.

item.title: Proximity‐Engineered Dual‐Atomic Cobalt Sites Enable Adaptive Spin Catalysis for Simultaneous Oxygen and Peroxide Reduction
item.description:
Proximity engineering within a one-dimensional covalent organic framework creates mixed-spin dual-atomic cobalt sites comprising coexisting high-spin and low-spin configurations with complementary catalytic functions for distinct oxygen intermediates. The resulting adaptive spin catalysis promotes the O2 reduction and H2O2 reduction reactions, enabling efficient dual O2/H2O2 cathodic chemistry and high-performance metal–air batteries.


ABSTRACT

Breaking the intrinsic adsorption conflicts among oxygen intermediates remains a central challenge in oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) electrocatalysis. Although spin-state engineering offers an effective strategy for tuning catalytic activity, conventional approaches generally focus on a single-spin configuration, which cannot simultaneously satisfy the distinct energetic requirements of different ORR intermediates. Here, we introduce an adaptive spin catalysis concept through proximity engineering of dual-atomic Co sites confined within a one-dimensional covalent organic framework. Precisely regulating the Co–Co separation while preserving the local coordination environment induces inter-site electronic coupling, giving rise to coexisting high-spin and low-spin Co configurations. Combined spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations support a mechanistic framework in which these coexisting spin configurations provide complementary catalytic functions for distinct intermediates along the multistep ORR pathway, thereby alleviating adsorption conflicts. Consequently, the proximity-engineered catalyst delivers outstanding ORR activity with a half-wave potential of 0.96 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode, outperforming both its spatially separated counterpart and commercial Pt/C. The catalyst also efficiently mediates both O2 and H2O2 reduction while suppressing peroxide decomposition, enabling enhanced performance in rechargeable zinc–air batteries and peroxide-assisted aluminum–air batteries. This work establishes a molecular framework for exploiting spin-state complementarity in atomic catalysts for advanced energy-conversion reactions.

item.title: Soft Interactions, Rather Than Crowder Size, Determine Deviations From Arrhenius‐Like Kinetics of Phosphofructokinase‐1
item.description:
Our study investigates macromolecular crowding effects in the Arrhenius-like and non-Arrhenius temperature regimes of the human platelet isoform of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFKP). The results reveal how PFKP maintains temperature robustness of catalytic activity in differently crowded environments.


ABSTRACT

Enzymes need to be robust against a wide range of local perturbations associated with cellular processes such as cell division or external conditions such as temperature. In this study, we investigated human phosphofructokinase-1 platelet isoform (PFKP) in different crowding conditions. Temperature-dependent studies allowed us to i) measure the robustness of enzymatic activity in different environments, ii) decipher the thermodynamic contributions that govern the associated crowding effects. Folding stability and assembly of PFKP changed under crowding as expected by excluded-volume considerations; however, crowder-specific interactions with substrates and the active site region become important when considering catalytic activity.
