Through evolutionary algorithms that constrain the generation direction of multi-property molecules, the framework enables up to 700-fold enrichment of rare quadruple-property candidates. This work provides a scalable pathway for multi-objective discovery in chemistry and materials science.

item.title: A DNA G‐Quadruplex‐Targeting Ligand Suppresses c‐MYC Expression: Implications for Gemcitabine‑Resistant Pancreatic Cancer
item.description:
PQB-4, a fluorescent small-molecule ligand that targets c-MYC DNA G-quadruplexes (G4s), showed marked synergy with gemcitabine in resistant PANC-1 cells (CI = 0.027). In vivo, the ligand reduced tumor weight by 44% in a PANC-1 xenograft model. These results highlight the therapeutic potential of c-MYC DNA G4-targeting ligands for treating gemcitabine-resistant pancreatic cancer.


ABSTRACT

The MYC oncogene is dysregulated in nearly 70% of human cancers and plays a central role in tumor initiation and progression. However, direct targeting of c-MYC remains challenging because of its “undruggable” nature. Stabilization of DNA G-quadruplex (G4) structures within the c-MYC promoter offers an alternative strategy to suppress c-MYC transcription. Here, we report the synthesis and biological evaluation of a series of styryl quinolinium ligands, identifying PQB-4 as a selective c-MYC DNA G4-binder (KD <1.0 µM). PQB-4 exhibited marked antiproliferative activity against pancreatic cancer cell lines, including MIA PaCa-2 (IC50 = 2.9 µM), PANC-1 (IC50 = 4.5 µM), and gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells (IC50 = 5.0 µM), while showing substantially lower toxicity toward noncancerous HK-2 cells (IC50 = 40.1 µM). Mechanistically, PQB-4 stabilized c-MYC DNA G4-structures, suppressed c-MYC mRNA and protein expression, induced G0/G1 cell-cycle arrest, and activated a p53-dependent DNA damage response. PQB-4 also promoted telomere damage, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, ferroptosis, and mitophagy, while inhibiting cancer cell migration, proliferation, and survival. Notably, PQB-4 synergized strongly with gemcitabine in resistant PANC-1 cells (CI = 0.027). In a PANC-1 xenograft model, PQB-4 reduced tumor weight by 44%. These findings highlight c-MYC DNA G4 targeting by PQB-4 as a feasible therapeutic strategy for pancreatic cancer, particularly in gemcitabine-resistant disease.

item.title: Click‐to‐Release Reactivity of Quaternary Anilinium Tetrazines Enables Cascade Assembly of Multifunctional Biomolecular Scaffolds
item.description:
Click chemistry has evolved from making covalent connections to also breaking bonds. Here, a cascade assembly is reported that combines these maneuvers to build multifunctional biomolecular scaffolds in a modular one-pot reaction. The unifying azide release-tetrazine hub clicks with a trans-cyclooctene tag, rapidly liberates N,N-dimethylaniline to generate a thiol trap in situ, and finishes by adding a strained alkyne building block, all in high yield.


ABSTRACT

Click chemistry has evolved from its origins in forming covalent connections to also include breaking bonds, cleaving linkers, and liberating cargo, creating broad applications in chemical biology and biomedicine. The reaction sequences that drive these tools are complex, and thus prone to an array of dead-end intermediates that reduce their release/cleavage efficiency. Here, we redirect that complexity to explore yet another aspect of tetrazine (Tz)/trans-cyclooctene (TCO) click-to-release. By exchanging the carbamate linkage of established release Tzs for an anilinium leaving group, post-click tautomerization is accelerated and temporally synchronized, generating an intermediate capable of trapping thiols rapidly and in high yields. Further integration of an orthogonal azide into the Tz hub enables a one-pot multi-component reaction that allows straightforward combinatorial synthesis of densely functionalized architectures. Leveraging both click and release, the resulting process converts a Tz/TCO pair into a ternary scaffold on demand, readily incorporating fluorophores, chelators, cleavable drugs, proteins, oligonucleotides, and more. This modular cascade assembly offers a rapid and versatile platform for functionalization of biomolecules and small molecule targeting vectors, with immediate potential in imaging, theranostics, and multivalent bioconjugate design.

item.title: Breaking the Additive Paradox in Aqueous Aluminum‐Ion Batteries via Weak‐Coordination Asymmetric Electrolyte Chemistry
item.description:
Beyond the trade-off: electrolyte optimization can redistribute rather than eliminate failure. In the weak-coordination asymmetric electrolyte (Al(OTf)3–DMSO–FEC), DMSO reconstructs the rigid Al3+ hydration environment but leaves a secondary dielectric/interfacial bottleneck, which is subsequently compensated by FEC through enhanced electrostatic screening and fluorinated interphase formation. This sequential resolution of coupled failure modes enables 2000 h reversible Al plating/stripping and 90.8% capacity retention after 2000 cycles.


ABSTRACT

Aqueous aluminum-ion batteries (AAIBs) are compelling for sustainable storage, yet the strong hydrolysis of Al3+ acidifies the electrolyte, causing corrosion and passivation that necessitate modification. Additives designed to break the rigid Al3+ solvation shell face a paradox: they often compromise reversibility via either dielectric collapse or kinetic deadlocks. Here, we break this paradox by establishing a weak-coordination asymmetric electrolyte based on aluminum trifluoromethanesulfonate (Al(OTF)3), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). DMSO coordinates to Al3+, displacing coordinated water to suppress water activity, but cannot preserve the dielectric environment. FEC compensates via three synergistic functions: high dielectric constant for electrostatic screening, weak hydrogen bonding for solvation asymmetry reinforcement, and reductive decomposition for solid electrolyte interphase(SEI) formation. The sequential coupling of DMSO-mediated solvation disruption with FEC-enables dielectric/interfacial compensation accelerates desolvation and stabilizes electrode: a fluorinated SEI enables 2000 h reversible Al plating/stripping, while a spinel-to-layer transformation creates a fluorinated interface on vanadium oxide with asymmetric channels, mitigating dissolution. The full cell retains 90.8% capacity after 2000 cycles at 4 A g−1. By showing that resolving one bottleneck can expose another, this work reframes additive optimization as sequential processes of identifying and compensating coupled failure mechanisms, generalizing a design principle for multivalent aqueous electrolytes.

item.title: The tRNA‐Modification Geranyl‐2‐Thiouridine Enables RNA‐Lipid Association
item.description:
We report the preparation of mono- to tri-geranylated RNA and the association of the hydrophobic RNA with membranes for future efficient incorporation of RNA into liposomes.


ABSTRACT

The packaging of RNA in lipid nanoparticles for protection and delivery was key for the development of mRNA vaccines and therapeutics. Formulation requires the addition of a variety of lipids (including cationic) in high amounts to form complexes with the negatively charged RNA. While this approach was successful for the development of RNA vaccines, it represents a major challenge for future developments. Increasing the lipophilicity of RNA is one possible approach to reducing the amount of lipid required. In nature, geranyl-2-thiouridine occurs at the “Wobble” position 34 of certain bacterial tRNAs. This work details investigations into geranylated oligonucleotides and their interactions with lipids. We developed an efficient post-synthetic procedure for oligonucleotide geranylation in aqueous solutions using a geranyl-sulfonium salt. We discovered that the geranyl-modification can be replaced by thiol-nucleophiles, enabling a reversible switch of the hydrophobic character of the oligonucleotides. We show that the geranyl-modified oligonucleotides anchor onto neutral membrane structures and oil droplets. Oligonucleotides bound to the outer surface of neutral liposomes can flip to the inner membrane surface by freeze-thaw cycles, leading to a protective effect against enzymatic or chemical degradation. Our work expands the scope of oligonucleotide lipidation strategies, which are of great interest in RNA delivery systems.
